title: Peaceful Queens
statement:
On an **n × n** chessboard you want to place **n** queens so that no two queens attack each other. A queen attacks every square in its row, its column and both of its diagonals.

Count the number of different placements. Two placements are different if some square has a queen in one placement and not in the other (rotations and reflections count as different placements).
output: Print one integer: the number of ways to place n non-attacking queens.

samples.explanation: The two solutions put the queens in columns 2 4 1 3 and 3 1 4 2 (row by row).

hints: Every row has exactly one queen. Place them row by row with recursion.
Remember which columns and diagonals are already used. On the diagonal going down-right, row - col is constant; on the other one, row + col is constant.
Backtracking: after the recursive call returns, remove the queen and try the next column.
editorial:
Backtracking. Place one queen per row. Keep three boolean arrays: used columns, used "row - col" diagonals and used "row + col" diagonals. In row r try every column c that is free in all three arrays, mark it, recurse into row r + 1 and unmark it afterwards. When r reaches n you found one placement. For n = 12 there are 14200 placements and the search visits well under a million states. Bit masks make it even faster: the free columns are `~(cols | d1 | d2)`.

Complexity: exponential, but heavily pruned; fast for n ≤ 12.
